text:
Many computer CPUs and subsystems were based on the 74181, including several historically significant models.

NOVA 1200 Introduced in 1970 by Data General, it was the first commercial 16-bit minicomputer to use the 74181. Curiously, it uses only one 74181, running the data through four times. The later Nova 800 uses four 74181s.[1]

Several models of the PDP-11[2] Most popular minicomputer of all time,[3] manufactured by Digital Equipment Corporation.

Xerox Alto The first computer to use the desktop metaphor and graphical user interface (GUI).[4,5]

VAX-11/780 The first VAX, the most popular 32-bit computer of the 1980s[3] manufactured by Digital Equipment Corp.[6]

Three Rivers PERQ A commercial computer workstation influenced by the Xerox Alto and first released in 1979.[7]

Computer Automation Naked Mini LSI-2 LSI is misused as a marketing hook. It did not use a LSI processor but rather four 74181s.[8]

KMC11 Peripheral processor for Digital Equipment Corporation PDP-11.[9]

FPP-12 Floating-point unit for the Digital Equipment Corporation PDP-12.[10]

Wang 2200 CPU (one 74181 per CPU)[11] and disk controller (two 74181s per controller)[12]

TI-980A/980B Texas Instruments 16-bit minicomputers.[13]

TI-990 Texas Instruments 16-bit minicomputers.[14]

Honeywell option 1100 The so-called "scientific unit" option for Honeywell H200/H2000 series mainframes.

Datapoint 2200 Version II used two 74181s[15] as did follow-on machines, the Datapoint 5500, 6600, and 1800/3800 The successors of the computer that defined the architecture for the Intel 8008.

Cogar System 4 / Singer 1501 / ICL 1501 Intelligent Terminal[16]

Varian Data Machines V70 series of 16-bit minicomputers

HP 2100 series About half the models in the series used four 74181s.

The ABLE 16-bit minicomputer from New England Digital, used as the processor for their Synclavier synthesizer, used four of these ALU chips.[17]
